idiom_name: plain predicate functions ((value) => boolean); a schema library (.refine) for reasons
implementation_notes: In JavaScript a validator is a function: (value) => boolean. contramap is calling a rule on a projection (const on = (project, rule) => v => rule(project(v))), divide and conquer are && and true, and choose is a switch on a discriminated field - no wrapper type or typeclass is needed, which is why the structure is invisible in JS code. A boolean carries no reason, so anything user-facing either returns a verdict object or defers to a schema library: zod's .refine/.superRefine attach reusable checks to a schema and safeParse returns every issue with its path, while the schema doubles as the shape contract.
pitfalls: Coercion makes predicates lie: value.length on a number, !value on the string '0', and NaN comparisons pass or fail for the wrong reasons - narrow on typeof/Number.isFinite before comparing.
Array.prototype.every/some short-circuit, so they cannot collect all failures; map to verdicts when the API must report every problem.
Truthiness of the rule value is a trap: a function returning false is still truthy, so if (rules.check) is not a validation - always call the rule explicitly.
